studySteps: Define the central ideas: Nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio data.
Use the UX scenario: Device categories, satisfaction ratings, temperature and task completion time.
Test your understanding: explain how the idea supports this objective: Recognise measurement scales, appropriate summaries and chart implications.
Write a short evidence-based explanation, cite the reading, and note at least one limitation.

definitions.meaning: A nominal variable distinguishes observations by their identity or category; there is no intrinsic greater-than or less-than relationship among its values. The categories should be mutually exclusive for a single-choice field, and any numbers used are identifiers, not quantities. In UX analytics, “mobile”, “desktop” and “tablet” are nominal, even if the database codes them as 1, 2 and 3. Appropriate summaries include counts, proportions and the most frequent category; an average of category codes is meaningless.

An ordinal variable puts categories into an interpretable sequence, but the gaps between adjacent ranks are not established as equal. A five-point ease scale orders “very difficult” through “very easy”, but the perceived jump from 1 to 2 need not match 4 to 5. Frequencies, medians and rank-based comparisons preserve this interpretation. Researchers sometimes average ratings for pragmatic reasons, especially across multi-item scales, but the extra equal-spacing assumption needs justification.

An interval variable has ordered values with equal units of difference: a five-unit change has the same size anywhere on the scale. Its zero is conventional, not the absence of the measured attribute, so ratios of raw values are not meaningful. Celsius temperature is the classic example: 30°C is 10°C warmer than 20°C but not “50% hotter”. Differences, means and standard deviations can be meaningful; multiplicative statements require a true-zero scale.

A ratio variable has equal intervals and a non-arbitrary zero representing none of the measured quantity. That allows both subtraction and multiplication comparisons. If one checkout task takes 20 seconds and another takes 40 seconds, the second duration is twice as long. Count of errors, number of attempts, elapsed time and distance are common UX ratio measures; check how values are collected and whether zero is a real possible observation.

lessons.explanation: The mathematical question is not whether a data field contains numbers, but what the numbers mean. A device code of 3 is still nominal. A five-category ease rating is ordinal because “very easy” follows “easy”, but the felt distance may vary. Celsius temperature is interval because the zero is conventional. Duration in seconds is ratio because zero means no elapsed duration. The scale restricts comparisons and influences visual encodings and statistics.
lessons.workedExample: In a checkout usability test, device=mobile/desktop (nominal), ease=very hard…very easy (ordinal), room temperature in °C (interval), and task completion seconds (ratio). Show device frequencies in a bar chart; retain ordered ease categories; plot durations on a numeric axis.
lessons.comparison: Ordinal versus interval: order alone does not justify subtracting neighbouring ratings as equal distances. Ratio versus interval: “twice as long” works for seconds, not Celsius degrees.
lessons.pitfall: Treating numeric category identifiers as measurements; saying a rating of 4 is necessarily twice the experience of 2.
lessons.practice: Classify device type, severity (low/medium/high), time in seconds, and temperature in °C. For each, state one valid and one invalid operation.
lessons.selfCheck: Device nominal; severity ordinal; time ratio; Celsius interval. A mean “device code” is invalid; ratio comparisons of time are meaningful.

lessons.title: Descriptive statistics
lessons.concepts: Mean, median, mode, spread and outliers
lessons.goal: Calculate common summaries and choose robust interpretations.
lessons.example: Compare checkout times with one unusually slow task.

readings.title: OpenIntro Statistics
readings.focus: Variables, data types and measurement scales

studySteps: Define the central ideas: Mean, median, mode, spread and outliers.
Use the UX scenario: Compare checkout times with one unusually slow task.
Test your understanding: explain how the idea supports this objective: Calculate common summaries and choose robust interpretations.
Write a short evidence-based explanation, cite the reading, and note at least one limitation.

definitions.meaning: The arithmetic mean is the sum of numeric observations divided by the number of observations. It uses every value and estimates a centre of the distribution, but unusual observations can move it substantially. If task times are 18, 20, 22, 24 and 116 seconds, the mean is 40 seconds. Report sample size and examine the distribution before calling it the “typical” user experience.

The median is the middle observation after numerical values are sorted; with an even number of values, it is the average of the two middle numeric values. It resists extreme observations better than the mean. For the checkout times 18, 20, 22, 24 and 116 seconds, the median is 22 seconds. Use it when a long right tail would make the mean less representative, but still investigate unusually slow users.

The mode is the most frequently observed value or category. It is especially useful for nominal survey answers such as preferred device or payment method, where an arithmetic mean makes no sense. A dataset can have multiple modes, or no useful unique mode if values rarely repeat. Report frequency counts alongside the mode so small differences are visible.

The range measures the total span between the largest and smallest numeric observations: maximum minus minimum. It is simple to interpret in task-time data, but depends only on two observations and can be inflated by one anomalous case. Pair it with the median, interquartile range or standard deviation for a more complete picture of variation.

Standard deviation quantifies how dispersed numerical observations are around their mean in the original unit of measurement. It is computed from squared deviations, then square-rooted; the sample version divides squared deviations by n − 1 before taking the root. A high SD in checkout time suggests heterogeneous experiences, but outliers and skew can dominate it. Always inspect the distribution rather than reading SD alone.

lessons.explanation: A summary is a compressed description, not a substitute for the underlying distribution. A single unusually long task can pull the mean upward, while the median remains more resistant. Always inspect shape, spread and the unit; consider the sample size before treating an average as product performance.
lessons.workedExample: Checkout times 18, 20, 22, 24 and 116 seconds give mean 40 seconds and median 22 seconds. A dashboard showing only the mean conceals that most participants were much faster and one participant struggled.
lessons.comparison: Mean versus median: both capture centre, but the median is less affected by an extreme time. Range versus SD: range uses only extremes; SD uses every observation.
lessons.pitfall: Reporting the mean as “typical” without checking outliers and distribution.
lessons.practice: Compute mean and median of 12, 14, 15, 19, 80; explain which tells the better user story.
lessons.selfCheck: Mean 28 seconds and median 15 seconds. The unusual 80-second result makes median useful, but investigate that user's problem.

lessons.goal: Match variable types to position, length, hue and area.

readings.focus: Exact free online book chapter; included quotation is attributed

readings.focus: Variables, data types and measurement scales

studySteps: Define the central ideas: Marks, channels, encodings and chart choice.
Use the UX scenario: Redesign a customer support dashboard.
Test your understanding: explain how the idea supports this objective: Match variable types to position, length, hue and area.
Write a short evidence-based explanation, cite the reading, and note at least one limitation.

definitions.meaning: A mark is a visible geometric element that represents one or more data items, such as a dot for a respondent, a bar for category count or a line connecting observations over time. Marks are the objects a reader sees; they do not acquire meaning until data is mapped to their visual properties. Choosing bars, points or lines should follow the question being asked, not stylistic preference.

A visual channel is a property of a mark that can carry information: x/y position, length, area, hue, lightness, orientation or shape. Different channels support different comparisons. Position along a shared numeric axis usually enables more precise magnitude comparisons than circle area; hue is usually better at distinguishing categories than showing exact quantities.

Visual encoding is the rule mapping a variable to a mark or channel. For example, a support dashboard may encode ticket count as bar length and ticket type as distinct categories along the y-axis. A sound encoding lets readers decode comparisons without guessing what colour or size means. Document your encoding decisions so the relationship between data, analytic task and graphic remains inspectable.

Graphical perception concerns the mental processes used to decode quantitative or categorical information from a graphic. Readers judge position, length, colour and area with different levels of accuracy. A pie chart may communicate composition, but small slice differences are harder to compare than aligned bars. Visualisations should be evaluated through the intended reading task, not only visual appeal.

lessons.explanation: Different encodings support different tasks. Position on a common scale makes exact comparison easy; length is powerful for quantities; hue is helpful for nominal groups; area is harder to compare precisely. A design is “good” only relative to its data, audience and question.
lessons.workedExample: For fraud cases by status, use a bar chart to compare counts. For how a backlog changes over 12 weeks, use a line chart. For relationships between turnaround time and case complexity, a scatterplot is more revealing than a pie chart.
lessons.comparison: Colour hue for categories versus colour lightness for magnitude: categories need distinction, amounts need an ordered progression.
lessons.pitfall: Using a pie chart to compare tiny differences in twenty case categories; encoding area instead of length without justification.
lessons.practice: Map category, amount, date and geographic location to suitable marks or channels. Explain your chosen comparison task.
lessons.selfCheck: Category→hue or separate bars; amount→position/length; date→position along ordered axis; location→map position if geography matters.

lessons.title: Research question anatomy
lessons.concepts: Questions, constructs, variables and operational definitions
lessons.goal: Turn fuzzy product concerns into measurable questions.
lessons.example: Define “ease of completing a claim” in observable terms.

readings.title: OpenIntro Statistics
readings.focus: Variables, data types and measurement scales

studySteps: Define the central ideas: Questions, constructs, variables and operational definitions.
Use the UX scenario: Define “ease of completing a claim” in observable terms.
Test your understanding: explain how the idea supports this objective: Turn fuzzy product concerns into measurable questions.
Write a short evidence-based explanation, cite the reading, and note at least one limitation.

definitions.meaning: A construct is an idea researchers want to study that cannot necessarily be observed directly, such as perceived trust, cognitive load or usability. It needs a theory of what the idea includes and what it excludes. Asking “is this interface trustworthy?” measures a response to a question, not trust itself in its entirety. Multiple indicators can improve coverage of complex constructs.

An operational definition specifies how an abstract construct is translated into a measurable observation. “Efficiency” might be operationalised as median task completion time in seconds for a clearly defined checkout task. The definition must state task, participants, measurement start/stop rules and exceptions. Other operationalisations could lead to different conclusions, so justify the one you choose.

A research question specifies the uncertainty a study intends to resolve, ideally naming the people, context, variables and comparison. “Is our app better?” is too broad; “Does a labelled filter reduce median retrieval time for claims officers compared with an icon-only filter?” can guide a concrete study. A research question is not automatically a causal claim: the design must permit the inference.

A variable is a property that can take different values across people, sessions, cases or time, such as device type, elapsed seconds or perceived difficulty. Its measurement scale determines sensible analysis. Distinguish a variable from its stored code, unit, collection procedure and potential confounds.

lessons.explanation: “Make claims easier” is a design aspiration, not a measurable research question. Specify who, what task, what intervention, what metric and under what context. An operational definition translates the idea into an observation, such as task success, time, error rate or a defined post-task rating. No single proxy captures every dimension of usability.
lessons.workedExample: Question: “Among new claims agents, does adding a guided form reduce omission errors compared with the current form?” Independent variable: form version. Outcome: omission errors per completed claim. Define what counts as an omission.
lessons.comparison: Construct validity versus measurement convenience: the easiest metric to collect may not capture the construct you care about.
lessons.pitfall: Claiming that higher screen views prove increased user confidence.
lessons.practice: Write a testable question about an investigation workflow. Define sample, comparison, metric, and one potential confound.
lessons.selfCheck: A strong answer defines an observable measure and explains why experience level or case difficulty could affect the outcome.

lessons.explanation: Visual attention is limited. Contrast, spatial grouping, consistent alignment and restrained highlighting direct attention. lessons.title: Sampling and representation
lessons.concepts: Population, sample, convenience bias and generalisability
lessons.goal: Explain when a convenience sample can mislead.
lessons.example: Recruit users for a mobile banking study.
studySteps: Define the central ideas: Population, sample, convenience bias and generalisability.
Use the UX scenario: Recruit users for a mobile banking study.
Test your understanding: explain how the idea supports this objective: Explain when a convenience sample can mislead.
Write a short evidence-based explanation, cite the reading, and note at least one limitation.

definitions.meaning: The population is the full group to which a research conclusion is intended to apply. For a claims dashboard evaluation, it might be all active claims officers at a defined organisation, not everyone who uses a web app. Specify eligibility and context, since generalising from five colleagues to an entire industry is not justified.

A sample is the subset of a population whose responses or behaviour are actually observed. Sample size matters, but the selection mechanism also matters: 300 volunteers can be less representative than a smaller well-selected group. Describe who participated, how they were recruited and who was excluded.

A sampling frame is the practical list or source from which eligible participants can be selected. A company directory could serve as a frame for staff research, but it may exclude temporary workers. Coverage gaps mean the frame does not perfectly represent the desired population.

Selection bias occurs when the mechanism determining who enters a dataset or group is related to the outcome being studied. Surveying only highly engaged power users may make a product seem easier to use than it is for new users. Random assignment to conditions does not by itself guarantee the recruited participants represent the wider population.

lessons.explanation: Large samples are not automatically representative. Surveying only active users tells us little about people who abandoned onboarding. Recruitment criteria and setting can matter more than sample size when the research question concerns a specialised group.
lessons.workedExample: A claims portal survey finds 90% satisfaction among 600 successful submitters. Users who failed to submit were never asked, creating a survivorship problem and limiting generalisability.
lessons.comparison: Random selection versus random assignment: selection concerns who participates; assignment concerns who receives each condition.
lessons.pitfall: Describing convenience respondents as representative of all users without evidence.
lessons.practice: Recruit eight participants for a claims form test. Specify inclusion criteria, recruitment channel and two populations not represented.
lessons.selfCheck: An honest plan identifies whose experience is missing and avoids population-wide conclusions.

lessons.title: Hypotheses and variables
lessons.concepts: Independent, dependent and confounding variables
lessons.goal: Write testable hypotheses with clear metrics.
studySteps: Define the central ideas: Independent, dependent and confounding variables.
Use the UX scenario: Compare two form designs.
Test your understanding: explain how the idea supports this objective: Write testable hypotheses with clear metrics.
Write a short evidence-based explanation, cite the reading, and note at least one limitation.

definitions.meaning: An independent variable is the factor whose variation or experimental manipulation is used to explain differences in an outcome. In an A/B test of two search-filter designs, filter type is the independent variable. Observing naturally different values is not the same as experimentally assigning them.

A dependent variable is the outcome measured in relation to predictors or conditions. In a checkout experiment, time-to-completion or error count might be dependent variables. Specify how they are recorded and whether the metric reflects the research question.

A confound is a third factor related to both the predictor or condition and the outcome, creating an alternative explanation. If expert users get design A and novices get design B, expertise may explain completion-time differences. Random assignment, matching or statistical adjustment may reduce confounding, but none automatically fixes every bias.

A hypothesis is a precise, testable expectation about a pattern or difference, derived from theory or observation. For example, “visible filter labels reduce median task time compared with icons alone” predicts a directional result. State the population, outcome and comparison; distinguish this research hypothesis from the statistical null hypothesis.

lessons.explanation: A good study separates the intervention from its outcome and asks what other factor could explain the result. In nonexperimental work, calling a variable “independent” doesn't establish causality. Write hypotheses that are falsifiable and state outcome measurement precisely.
lessons.workedExample: Hypothesis: guided field validation decreases missing attachments. Version type predicts omission count; case complexity and employee tenure might affect both interface selection and errors.
lessons.comparison: Predictor versus cause: finding an association does not prove intervention effect.
lessons.pitfall: Concluding a new UI caused faster completion when the new group also handled easier cases.
lessons.practice: Identify IV, DV and two confounds for comparing a guided vs unassisted investigation form.
lessons.selfCheck: IV form type; DV omission errors or duration; confounds could include case complexity and agent experience.

lessons.title: Measurement and quality
lessons.concepts: Reliability, validity and construct definition
lessons.goal: Distinguish a repeatable metric from one that measures the right construct.
studySteps: Define the central ideas: Reliability, validity and construct definition.
Use the UX scenario: Evaluate “engagement” via session time.
Test your understanding: explain how the idea supports this objective: Distinguish a repeatable metric from one that measures the right construct.
Write a short evidence-based explanation, cite the reading, and note at least one limitation.

definitions.meaning: Reliability is the consistency of a measurement under comparable conditions. An instrument may produce similar scores on repeated administrations while still measuring the wrong thing. For usability coding, clear definitions and agreement between independent coders can improve reliability.

Construct validity concerns whether a chosen measure or manipulation adequately represents the intended concept. A one-item satisfaction question may capture overall sentiment but not learnability or efficiency. Argue from theory, evidence and multiple indicators rather than treating the metric label as proof.

Internal validity concerns whether the study design supports a credible conclusion that the tested factor caused the observed outcome, rather than a confound or alternative event. Random assignment and controls can help in experiments. A simple before-after comparison is vulnerable to practice effects and external changes.

External validity concerns whether findings generalise beyond the observed sample, tasks and setting. A laboratory result on a desktop prototype may not transfer to mobile users in a noisy field environment. Describe the population and circumstances for which the claim is warranted.

lessons.explanation: Reliable does not mean valid: a stopwatch can consistently measure task duration but may not capture confidence. Distinguish measurement quality from causal inference and generalisability. Definitions and coding protocols reduce ambiguity and improve repeatability.
lessons.workedExample: Two observers count “form errors”; one counts only mandatory field omissions, the other counts every correction. Their disagreement is a reliability problem. Neither count alone fully measures trust in the form.
lessons.comparison: Reliability versus validity: consistent results can consistently measure the wrong thing.
lessons.pitfall: Claiming a short survey is valid only because responses agree with one another.
lessons.practice: Create operational definitions for “error”, “confidence” and “success”. Explain how to check quality.
lessons.selfCheck: Specify clear counting rules, triangulate measures where possible and identify sources of disagreement.

lessons.concepts: Random assignment, control and intervention

studySteps: Define the central ideas: Random assignment, control and intervention.

definitions.meaning: Random assignment uses a chance mechanism to allocate recruited participants to experimental conditions, helping balance known and unknown confounds across groups. It differs from random sampling, which concerns how people are selected from a population. Assignment improves causal comparisons, but does not automatically make a sample representative.

A control or comparison group provides a reference outcome against which to evaluate an intervention. It may use the existing design, an alternative design or no treatment, depending on the research question. The comparison must be sufficiently similar in circumstances to support interpretation.

Treatment means manipulated interface or procedure. In this lesson, it helps you examine the question: Explain why random assignment helps isolate an effect. For example, consider this UX research situation: Plan an A/B study of navigation. Do not assume this term alone proves the design is effective; identify which observation or comparison would support the claim, and note a plausible limitation. A useful distinction to keep in mind is: Random sampling versus random assignment: the first affects representativeness; the second supports causal inference within the study.

Blinding means keeping relevant group information hidden where feasible to reduce bias. In this lesson, it helps you examine the question: Explain why random assignment helps isolate an effect. For example, consider this UX research situation: Plan an A/B study of navigation. Do not assume this term alone proves the design is effective; identify which observation or comparison would support the claim, and note a plausible limitation. A useful distinction to keep in mind is: Random sampling versus random assignment: the first affects representativeness; the second supports causal inference within the study.

lessons.explanation: In an experiment, deliberately vary one relevant factor and hold other conditions sufficiently comparable. Random assignment reduces systematic group differences on average; it does not guarantee perfectly balanced small samples. Keep a clear task, standardised instructions and preregistered outcome definitions.
lessons.workedExample: Randomly show 40 recruits either old or new claim form; compare omission rates after the same task. If the new form receives more experienced recruits, allocation may have failed or sampling is small.
lessons.comparison: Random sampling versus random assignment: the first affects representativeness; the second supports causal inference within the study.
lessons.pitfall: Changing button language, layout and case difficulty together and attributing effects to only the button.
lessons.practice: Design a randomised comparison with clear assignment, outcome, control and an ethical stopping rule.
lessons.selfCheck: Good protocol holds task conditions comparable and records deviations.

definitions.meaning: Sampling distribution means distribution of a statistic across hypothetical repeated samples. In this lesson, it helps you examine the question: Explain uncertainty without claiming a probability about a fixed parameter. For example, consider this UX research situation: Interpret a conversion-rate interval. Do not assume this term alone proves the design is effective; identify which observation or comparison would support the claim, and note a plausible limitation. A useful distinction to keep in mind is: Standard deviation versus standard error: SD describes individual variability; SE describes precision of an estimated statistic.

Standard error means estimated variability of a statistic across samples. In this lesson, it helps you examine the question: Explain uncertainty without claiming a probability about a fixed parameter. For example, consider this UX research situation: Interpret a conversion-rate interval. Do not assume this term alone proves the design is effective; identify which observation or comparison would support the claim, and note a plausible limitation. A useful distinction to keep in mind is: Standard deviation versus standard error: SD describes individual variability; SE describes precision of an estimated statistic.

A confidence interval is produced by a method that, over many hypothetical repeated samples under its assumptions, captures the fixed population parameter at a stated rate (often 95%). It describes uncertainty in estimation, not a 95% probability that this one realised interval contains the parameter. Width depends on variation, sample size and method.

Margin of error means approximate uncertainty extent under specified assumptions. In this lesson, it helps you examine the question: Explain uncertainty without claiming a probability about a fixed parameter. For example, consider this UX research situation: Interpret a conversion-rate interval. Do not assume this term alone proves the design is effective; identify which observation or comparison would support the claim, and note a plausible limitation. A useful distinction to keep in mind is: Standard deviation versus standard error: SD describes individual variability; SE describes precision of an estimated statistic.

lessons.explanation: An estimate is not exact. A 95% confidence interval means that the procedure would cover the fixed population parameter in about 95% of repeated studies under its assumptions; it is not a 95% probability assigned to this particular fixed parameter in the frequentist framework. Larger representative samples often narrow intervals, though design and variability matter.
lessons.workedExample: A sample estimates 72% of users completed onboarding, with a 95% interval of 65–79%. That suggests uncertainty in the population completion rate, not that 72% is guaranteed.
lessons.comparison: Standard deviation versus standard error: SD describes individual variability; SE describes precision of an estimated statistic.
lessons.pitfall: Reading a confidence interval as the range containing 95% of individual users.
lessons.practice: Explain what 65–79% means without saying there is a 95% chance the fixed parameter lies inside.
lessons.selfCheck: Repeated-study coverage is the intended interpretation under assumptions.

Residual means difference between observed and model-predicted value. In this lesson, it helps you examine the question: Distinguish association, prediction and causation. definitions.meaning: Chart integrity means faithfully representing quantities and relationships without misleading scales, selective exclusions or deceptive encodings. A truncated bar-chart axis can magnify a small difference, while a missing denominator can disguise changes in rates. An ethical chart should let a reader trace the claim back to the measurements.

Hierarchy means relative prominence of analytical elements. In this lesson, it helps you examine the question: Critique from evidence and reader goals. Annotation means context attached to a data feature. In this lesson, it helps you examine the question: Critique from evidence and reader goals. Do not assume this term alone proves the design is effective; identify which observation or comparison would support the claim, and note a plausible limitation. Accessibility in data visualisation means making structure, values and intended meaning perceivable and operable for diverse users, including people using assistive technology or with colour-vision differences. Use readable contrasts, direct labels, keyboard interaction and textual summaries; avoid using hue alone to communicate an essential category.

lessons.explanation: Critique a chart by separating accuracy, accessibility and usefulness. Ask whether the chart claims more than the data can support, whether scales mislead, whether colour is the sole communication channel, and whether uncertainty is visible. A beautiful chart can still hide essential context.

lessonNotes.1.1:
So mostly here what was there to takeaway is the 4 levels of measurements, 
1. Nominal - This is division in mostly categorical sects, this can be like groups or some sort of collective unit enveloping a range. Like Blood groups or Devices used. These are not is a specific order. Mostly represented by Bar graphs or pie charts. Basically one bucket per category.
2. Ordinal - Here this are in a ranked order and cant be altered, but the gaps between ranks aren't necessarily equal. For instance, satisfaction ratings like poor, fair, good, excellent or class rankings or priority levels. Ordinal data often uses ordered bars or stacked bars or heatmaps. But the key is the sequence. 

So you'd never shuffle the order randomly of the bars. And you wouldn't use an average or mean over nominal or ordinal data, but medians or modes can work depending on what you're trying to convey.
